Before you start

Each slide carries its own point, so you can talk with the room instead of reading notes. Frame everything as a method problem, never a smarts problem. Nobody shares grades or how long they studied. Expect pushback on learning styles: preferring visuals is fine, it just doesn’t change how people learn.

Every student in the room

The brain dump can be typed, spoken, drawn or written in any language, and "who quizzes you" can be a sibling, a friend on a call, or flashcards, since not every student has a parent home or a quiet room.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students can explain why rereading feels like studying but holds up worst (familiar isn't the same as knowing), use three methods that work (quiz yourself, space it out, mix it up), and sketch a spaced plan for a real test coming up. The aim is a better method. Nobody should leave thinking they're bad at school.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • The take-home link to share after the talk

Flow

  1. 6 minThree myths, one per slide
  2. 6 minThe experiment, and familiar feels like knowing
  3. 6 minHard reps, and mixing it up
  4. 6 minBrain dump out loud: turn and talk, share out
  5. 10 minWhich plan would you change? Eli, Sofia, Sam
  6. 5 minTen days out, five short sessions
  7. 6 minEvery student, where else this shows up, close

Short on time (20-minute advisory)

Two myths, the experiment, hard reps, the brain dump turn and talk, one of the three plans, the ten-day plan, and the close.

Before you teach
Some students already feel behind.

First Upper School tests can shake students who did well before. Frame everything as a method problem, never a smarts problem. A student who rereads has been doing what most students do.

Keep grades and scores private.

Don't ask anyone to share a test score or how long they studied. The brain dump stays with the student. Nobody hands it in.

Expect pushback on learning styles.

Many students have been told they're visual learners. Preferring visuals is fine. The research says matching teaching to a style doesn't improve learning. Say it gently and move on. Nobody needs correcting in front of the room.

Be honest about the research.

Most of these studies were with college students, and the math-mixing study was small. Methods raise the odds. They don't promise a grade. Students trust you more when you say so.

Good methods and still struggling.

If reading, writing or focusing takes a student much longer than it seems to take others, connect them with the learning specialist or a counselor. An evaluation can open up supports now and in college.

When stress is the bigger problem.

If a student says school stress is taking over their evenings, sleep or mood, thank them and walk them to a counselor that day. Don't work through it in front of the class.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Learning differences and disability.

The brain dump can be typed, spoken quietly into a phone, drawn as a map, or written as a list. Students with ADHD, dyslexia or slower processing may need more time on every activity. Measure what they can pull from memory, at whatever speed.

Not every student has the same study time.

Some students work, ride a long bus, or watch younger siblings after school. "Count questions, not hours" helps here: short quizzing sessions fit a tight evening. Every method in this lesson is free, and released practice questions are free online.

A quiet place isn't a given.

Some students share a room or study in a busy kitchen. Mention the school library and any after-school study space. A brain dump works on a bus or in a hallway.

Who quizzes you can be anyone.

Don't assume a parent is home to help. A sibling, a grandparent, a friend on a call, or a stack of flashcards all work. Sofia's scenario has a grandmother in it; swap in whatever fits your students.

Families hold different views on effort.

For some families, long hours at the desk are how effort shows. Respect that. The point is to make those hours count. Ask students how studying is talked about at home, as a private thought.

Language and the calendar.

Students learning English can brain dump in any language, then check against notes in English. Religious holidays, fasting and family events can block whole days; a spaced plan moves around them more easily than a cram can.

What the research says

Students who reread a passage did best on a test five minutes later. Students who read it once and then wrote down all they could remember beat them by 14 points at two days and at one week. The rereaders predicted they'd remember the most and remembered the least.

Roediger and Karpicke, Psychological Science, 2006

A review of hundreds of studies on ten common study techniques rated only two "high utility": practice testing and spreading study out over time. Rereading, highlighting and summarizing rated low.

Dunlosky et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2013

About 84% of college students said they reread notes or textbooks to study. About 11% practiced recalling information, and only 1% called that their main method.

Karpicke, Butler and Roediger, Memory, 2009

"Desirable difficulties": recalling from memory, waiting between sessions and mixing problem types feel slower in the moment, and that effort builds memory you can use later.

Bjork, 1994

Students who practiced math problems in blocks got 89% right during practice versus 60% for mixed practice. A week later the mixed group scored 63% and the blocked group 20%. A small study; mixed practice has held up in classrooms since.

Rohrer and Taylor, Instructional Science, 2007

In a study of more than 1,350 people, the best gap between study sessions grew with the time until the test: a day or two for a test a week away, closer to a month for a test a year away.

Cepeda et al., Psychological Science, 2008

During sleep the brain replays and strengthens what was learned that day. Sleep is an active part of memory consolidation.

Diekelmann and Born, Nature Reviews Neuroscience, 2010

No good evidence that teaching to a person's preferred "learning style" improves learning.

Pashler et al., Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 2008
